body:
| | | Hi Peter, **The Supreme Court issued an important elections ruling today** , so I’m back with a legalese-free update. In March, Trump issued an executive order. It had a directive to USPS, which is the saga you’ve seen at least a dozen emails from me about over the past six months. The Supreme Court finally shut that down for this election earlier this month. The other directive was to the Department of Homeland Security, and it was to create a voter citizenship verification system. DHS decided to expand a system called SAVE (which is different than the SAVE Act!) by connecting it to other datasets, like social security and passports. More importantly, they made this system searchable, the idea being that election officials could search their voter rolls for noncitizens. **Several states that eagerly tried this learned the hard way that the DHS data is incredibly inaccurate when few or none of the voters it flagged turned out to actually be noncitizens.** Lower courts stopped these bulk searches while lawsuits play out. Today the Supreme Court reinstated them. They didn’t say the system itself is legal, and in fact indicated it likely is causing harm to citizens, but said it can still be used while those lawsuits move through the legal system. **What does this mean for voters?** The ruling itself is clear that federal law about purging voters from voter rolls still applies, so states cannot use this to start removing voters. In Colorado, election officials have already rejected the delusional lies about noncitizen voters that started this whole thing. So no thank you, DOJ, we do not want or need your help managing our voter rolls. **I will fiercely protect voters from paying the price for this federal government’s manufactured crisis.** Which is why it’s so important that when a new Secretary of State enters the office in January, it’s **someone who wants to keep voters on the registration li****st, not take people off it.** We’re in the final stretch here. You’ve given me so much hope and support and the belief that we can take our democracy back. clean_body: | | | Hi Peter, The Supreme Court issued an important elections ruling today , so I’m back with a legalese-free update. In March, Trump issued an executive order. It had a directive to USPS, which is the saga you’ve seen at least a dozen emails from me about over the past six months. The Supreme Court finally shut that down for this election earlier this month. The other directive was to the Department of Homeland Security, and it was to create a voter citizenship verification system. DHS decided to expand a system called SAVE (which is different than the SAVE Act!) by connecting it to other datasets, like social security and passports. More importantly, they made this system searchable, the idea being that election officials could search their voter rolls for noncitizens. Several states that eagerly tried this learned the hard way that the DHS data is incredibly inaccurate when few or none of the voters it flagged turned out to actually be noncitizens. Lower courts stopped these bulk searches while lawsuits play out. Today the Supreme Court reinstated them. They didn’t say the system itself is legal, and in fact indicated it likely is causing harm to citizens, but said it can still be used while those lawsuits move through the legal system. What does this mean for voters? The ruling itself is clear that federal law about purging voters from voter rolls still applies, so states cannot use this to start removing voters. In Colorado, election officials have already rejected the delusional lies about noncitizen voters that started this whole thing. So no thank you, DOJ, we do not want or need your help managing our voter rolls. I will fiercely protect voters from paying the price for this federal government’s manufactured crisis. Which is why it’s so important that when a new Secretary of State enters the office in January, it’s someone who wants to keep voters on the registration list, not take people off it. We’re in the final stretch here. You’ve given me so much hope and support and the belief that we can take our democracy back. In solidarity, Amanda Gonzalez Democratic Nominee for Colorado Secretary of State | | ---|--- Paid for by Amanda for Colorado. Registered Agent Ashton Narzisi. | | Sent via . Peter, It's Becca. Can we talk about projection for a second? Because I've got to get this off my chest. You know the story of the boy who cried wolf? _Well, in this email, the boy is also the wolf._ **See, whenever this president accuses someone else of being a socialist, a communist, a threat to democracy, pay close attention. More often than not, he's describing exactly what he's doing himself.** Two examples, both from just this past week. He launched something called Trump TV: a 24/7 taxpayer-funded stream of nothing but him, his speeches, his events, on a loop. Yet, that's the EXACT kind of state-run media he claims only dictators create. On top of that, he used our tax dollars, yours and mine, to cut a campaign ad for himself ahead of the midterms when he isn’t even on the ballot. **Using taxpayer money to build yourself a personal television network and fund your own campaign ads is absolutely outrageous, full stop.** [_**If you agree and you are sick of this administration stealing your hard earned money – let’s change it! Well, in this email, the boy is also the wolf. See, whenever this president accuses someone else of being a socialist, a communist, a threat to democracy, pay close attention. More often than not, he's describing exactly what he's doing himself. Two examples, both from just this past week. He launched something called Trump TV: a 24/7 taxpayer-funded stream of nothing but him, his speeches, his events, on a loop. Yet, that's the EXACT kind of state-run media he claims only dictators create. On top of that, he used our tax dollars, yours and mine, to cut a campaign ad for himself ahead of the midterms when he isn’t even on the ballot. Using taxpayer money to build yourself a personal television network and fund your own campaign ads is absolutely outrageous, full stop. = = Here's the pattern I want everyone to start noticing, because once you see it, you can’t unsee it. When Trump accuses the other side of doing something, the first thing to check is whether he's already doing it himself. That's the tell. Because 9 times out of 10 – he's already beat everyone to the punch. Somebody has to actually say that out loud, especially with 39 days left before voters get the final word before these mid-term elections. = = In the original story, everyone stopped believing the boy after enough false alarms. In this one, the danger was never somewhere else. It's been him the whole time. Wars he started. Rent, groceries, and healthcare that keep getting further out of reach. ## CODY WAS BORN FOR THIS!
---
Cody Hart, Republican Candidate for Skagit County Sheriff, is excited to bring his work ethic and dedication to serving the community to Skagit County Marine Patrol. **"As a Navy Veteran, I have always had a passion for spending time on the water, safe boating, and marine life. I am excited to bring my years of experience on the water in the Puget Sound, rivers, and lakes across Skagit County to the Skagit County Sheriff office." according to Ha** rt. The Skagit County Sheriff's Office boat patrol unit consists of five, fulltime, commissioned sheriff's deputies and one patrol sergeant. This unit is responsible for all sheriff's office responsibilities on the waters of Skagit County. The deputies are assigned on a part-time basis to the boat patrol unit and are available to respond as the situation requires. In addition, these same deputies are regularly scheduled for weekend boat patrol in the summer months between the Memorial and Labor Day holidays. Cody went on to say, "The more I think about it, the more I believe I was born for this job". **Cody Hart for Government Accountability**

Ro Khanna [posted](https://substack.com/@rokhannausa/note/c-344511352?utm_source=notes-share-action&r=3zafez) five things Democrats will do in January if they win back the House: Raise the minimum wage. Pass paid family leave. End the war in Iran. Hold a vote on Medicare for All. Tax the billionaires.
I read it twice. I agreed with every item on it. And then I was left looking at the enormous empty space _around_ it.
These are good ideas. A functioning center-left government should have been pursuing all of them years ago. My reaction was simpler:
_**Yes, obviously. And then what?**_
Americans are living through war, mass surveillance, extraordinary concentrations of economic power, ecological breakdown, and a steady erosion of the constitutional restraints that are supposed to protect us from all of it. We are being asked to meet that moment with our time, our money, our doors knocked, our neighbors protected, our nerves held together.
And in return: five bullet points.
To be clear, I respect who I'm talking to. Khanna was the first member of Congress to sign Track AIPAC's PEACE Pledge, committing himself on military aid, war-crimes accountability, foreign influence, campaign finance and First Amendment protections. I signed it too.
So I'm not writing this because I think Ro Khanna has never thought past a talking point. I'm writing it partly because I think he has.
**Which is exactly why five feels so small.**

## What is power for?
Somewhere along the way, American political communication reduced the idea of governing to a consumer menu.
Paid leave. A tax credit. Cheaper insulin. A housing subsidy.
People need these things. They matter. **But governing is not the same thing as dispensing benefits.**
Government also decides whether the law reaches powerful people. Whether private corporations can accumulate so much control over housing, information, land, technology, medicine, money and political speech that ordinary people lose meaningful choices. Whether public institutions retain enough skill and capacity to solve anything. Whether war remains an ordinary instrument of policy. Whether constitutional rights mean anything when protecting them becomes inconvenient. Whether a person encountering the state meets a public servant, a contractor, an algorithm, a soldier, a prison guard--or nobody at all.
Five good policies are not the same thing as a theory of government.
When I first replied to Khanna's note, I rattled off nearly forty things I wanted to see.
That list, dashed off the top of my head in passionate frustration, was a howl more than a program, and I'll own that.
But when I looked back at it, nearly everything I had written was asking the same few questions.
**Who is power accountable to?**
**What must remain public?**
**What should no private actor be allowed to control?**
**What do we owe one another?**
_**And what, exactly, is government for?**_
[ Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9tZWxpc3NhNGNvbmdyZXNzLnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.LkMeZup1UKUvAv5VkhBqkIwYA2BpJrLbUryEcSoJ7j0?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=217343367)
## 1\. Make power answerable
A society does not have the rule of law because it prosecutes poor people efficiently.
It has the rule of law when the law can reach **upward**.
That means imposing serious consequences on war crimes committed in our name. Financial crimes capable of wrecking millions of households. Sexual abuse and trafficking protected by wealth or access. Corruption in federal contracting. Unlawful government surveillance. Election crimes. Abuse of public office.
Congress does not prosecute people. The executive branch does.
But a House majority is hardly powerless. House committees can investigate, hold hearings, take testimony, demand records and issue subpoenas within their jurisdiction; the House also controls its own rules and holds the constitutional power of impeachment.
The relevant question in January is not whether House Democrats can personally indict anyone.
**It is whether they intend to use the powers they actually hold** when wealth, office or political connection has provided years of practical impunity.
That same principle applies to democracy itself.
Democrats can promise better outcomes all day. Those promises still have to pass through a political system in which **concentrated wealth can exercise extraordinary influence over who runs, who gets heard, who survives a primary, what becomes politically possible, and what ever reaches a vote.**
Fixing _that,_ means addressing campaign finance. Dark money. Congressional ethics. Enforceable ethics rules for the Supreme Court. Voting rights. Election administration. Foreign-agent and foreign-influence laws enforced according to the same rules regardless of whose interests are involved.
Khanna has already signed a pledge that names campaign-finance reform and reducing corporate and special-interest influence as democratic priorities.
So I'm not asking why he omitted my favorite policies.
I'm asking something more basic:
**If we know political power is being distorted before policy ever reaches the floor, what are we prepared to do about it?**
Because every other promise rests on the answer.

## 2\. Rebuild public power -- and put limits on private power
We've now spent forty years privatizing not just services, but **powers**.
Incarceration. Surveillance. Parts of war-making and intelligence gathering. Public communications infrastructure. Financial infrastructure. Enormous stores of information about our movements, purchases, relationships and faces. These capabilities and this information is held in private hands, now, and operated for private profit, not public benefit. That's an extremely dangerous condition.
At the same time, we hollowed out many of the institutions that were supposed to act in the public interest.
Look at the EPA. USAID. SNAP. Infrastructure. Social Security administration. Public lands protection. Regulatory agencies that struggle to oversee industries whose lawyers and technical staffs can dwarf their own.
Then notice the trap.
Government becomes too understaffed, too brittle and too stripped of institutional knowledge to do something well. Its failure becomes evidence that government cannot work. Another function is outsourced. Public capacity weakens again.
Eventually people experience the state as simultaneously enormous and helpless: powerful enough to punish, search, detain or surveil them, but somehow incapable of making housing affordable, building a train, processing an application, protecting a river or stopping a monopoly.
That is not a healthy balance of power.
**I want a government strong enough to serve the public and strong enough to tell private power no.**
That does not mean government should run everything.
It means 1. Accountability matters, and 2. **Nobody should be completely captive to a private tollbooth for something necessary to participate in modern life.**
There is no reason whatsoever that government cannot institute a public option for public goods, funded with public dollars. (No good reason, that is. Lobbying, is the reason, and **institutionalized bribery is the opposite of a healthy rationale.**)
Healthcare is the obvious example of an industry where we desperately need a public option to protect Americans. But also consider broadband. Basic banking. Payments infrastructure. Essential pharmaceuticals. Utilities. Insurance. Transportation.
In some sectors the answer may be regulation. In others, antitrust. In others, cooperatives or public options.
The form can vary. The principle should not.
And we need the same seriousness around the companies selling government its coercive technologies. Palantir, Flock, Axon, Anduril and others are not ordinary office-supply vendors. They sell systems for surveillance, identification, policing, intelligence and military operations that ordinary citizens may have very little meaningful ability to inspect, challenge or escape.
**That should trigger democratic oversight and regulatory scrutiny proportionate to the power involved.**
So should for-profit incarceration. Surveillance pricing. Algorithmic wage discrimination. Corporate concentration of farmland. Locked-down vehicles and equipment people supposedly own but cannot repair.
And AI belongs here too.
If companies can produce dramatically more with dramatically fewer workers, the central political question is not whether the technology is impressive.
It is who gets the gain and who absorbs the loss.
**We cannot allow productivity gains to be privately captured while displacement becomes everyone else 's problem.**
That means we need to start talking seriously about a guaranteed income floor. About Social Security financing--ending the cap on contributions, for starters. About ownership of data. About monopolies. About the water, land and electricity consumed by enormous data centers. About what happens when a small number of firms control the computational infrastructure beneath much of the economy.
Those are not questions for _after_ the disruption arrives.
**Government exists partly so a society can see a foreseeable problem coming and choose not to drive directly into it.**

## 3\. End the machine that makes wars
Ending the war in Iran is on Khanna's list, and it should be. The United States is now months into that conflict, diesel in my area is above $7/gallon, and Congress has repeatedly wrestled with efforts to reassert its war powers.
But ending a war is an event.
**Ending the machinery that reliably** _**produces**_**wars is governance.**
Because otherwise - _what prevents the next Iran?_
The answer should be: Congress actually enforcing its constitutional war powers. Pentagon procurement that answers to taxpayers rather than contractors. Military aid constrained by law. Serious civilian oversight. Arms-control diplomacy.
And an unsparing look at the financial relationship between defense contractors, lobbyists, campaigns and the lawmakers responsible for deciding when and how America uses force.
**Otherwise every war we end simply leaves the machinery in place for the next one.**
Americans have been told, over and over again, that this particular war is exceptional. This particular enemy is uniquely dangerous. This particular emergency requires powers we would never tolerate under ordinary circumstances.
After enough exceptions, you have a system.
And systems reproduce what they are built to produce.

## 4\. A principled foreign policy: one standard for all
I wrote "Free Palestine" in my original reply, and I mean it.
In governing terms, that means _**at bare minimum:**_ Palestinian freedom and political rights; **reparations paid by Israel for their ongoing genocide and displacement of the Palestinians;** unfettered humanitarian access including by sea; military aid withdrawn immediately, any future aid of any kind conditioned on compliance with American and international law; meaningful arms-transfer standards; real, criminal, national and international accountability for war crimes, with teeth; and an end to American material support for atrocities **regardless of who commits them.**
Palestine is the essential example, but this principle does not end there.
**If human rights disappear whenever honoring them becomes geopolitically inconvenient, they were never principles.**
They were branding.
Iran. Palestine. Cuba. Sudan. Authoritarian governments we oppose. Authoritarian governments we call partners. Sanctions. Arms sales. International institutions. Climate commitments.
The countries and circumstances differ. The rule should survive the difference.
American power will never be morally perfect. No state's is.
But we can at least decide that law applies when it is inconvenient, that civilians do not become expendable because of the passport they hold, and that we will not describe conduct as monstrous when an adversary does it and regrettable when an ally does.
That is what having principles means.
And it applies at home too.

## 5\. Some debts cannot be paid with a tax credit
America's reckoning with our own past is **long overdue.** And there are serious outstanding obligations that we have not handled yet.
Reproductive freedom written into law. Equal rights for women. A serious national reckoning with reparations. Police accountable to the communities they serve. An end to routine militarization of domestic law enforcement. Real protection against violence directed at Muslims, immigrants, Black Americans, religious minorities and anyone else targeted because somebody has decided their difference makes them disposable.
And yes: **abolishing ICE.**
These are not primarily spending programs. They are questions of belonging and equal citizenship.
_**Who receives the protection of the American state?**_
_**Who mainly experiences its coercive power?**_
My family knows something about that question from the inside.
My husband, a U.S. military veteran and wheelchair user, spent 124 days in ICE detention. We fought in four federal jurisdictions without lawyers. Eventually a federal judge ordered his immediate release, calling his detention "flat out wrong."
But my husband had something many detained people do not: a family able to keep fighting, records we could assemble, people watching, and eventually a federal court willing to hear us.
**What happens to the person nobody is watching?**
That is the question I carried out of those 124 days.
_A governing program that talks beautifully about what government can give people, but says little about what government must never be permitted to do to them, is incomplete._

## January is not magic
There is an obvious objection to everything I have just written.
"A Democratic House cannot just _**do**_ all of this."
Correct.
If Democrats win the House this November, they will not control the entire federal government. A House majority cannot wave its hand in January and enact Medicare for All, restructure campaign finance, abolish ICE, regulate AI, repair the administrative state, rewrite foreign policy and pass an entire generation's worth of unfinished civil-rights legislation.
I am not asking it to.
But a House majority **can** hold hearings. Investigate. Subpoena. Write bills. Build coalitions. Put proposals on paper. Force recorded votes. Fight over appropriations. Put abuses into the public record. Make members of Congress tell their constituents, on the record, where they stand.
And it can spend two years preparing an **actual governing program** for the next time the public hands Democrats enough power to enact one.
I don't expect a House majority to accomplish all of this in January.
**I expect it to know where it is trying to take the country, and to tell us.**
**Clearly. Unapologetically. With just as much detail as the Heritage Foundation put into Project 2025.**
That is a much lower bar than instant transformation.
It is also _much_ higher than five bullet points.

## A fight needs a destination
Here is the part I most want Khanna, and every Democrat asking for our votes and our effort, to hear.
**Millions** of Americans have spent these years marching, organizing, donating, knocking doors, sitting through meetings, defending their neighbors from raids, reporting abuses, unionizing workplaces, protecting migrants and building mutual-aid networks from scratch.
The fierce public already exists.
DC, and folks aspiring to be there, **should not mistake our dedication and endurance for an inexhaustible resource.**
Movements eventually ask a question:
_Toward what?_
You cannot organize a population forever around preventing catastrophe.
"Stop the worst thing from happening" is an emergency instruction.
It is not a vision of a civilization.
**People will defend institutions far more fiercely when those institutions visibly defend them.** People will endure sacrifice when they can see what the sacrifice is for. And people who have spent years fighting merely to hold the line are entitled to ask where, eventually, we intend to go.
So, Ro:
Your five are good.
**Now give us fifty.**
Not fifty bills -- give us the _**principles**_.
Give us the structural reforms you will fight for. The abuses you intend to investigate. The institutions you intend to rebuild. The concentrations of power you believe no democracy should tolerate. The rights you consider non-negotiable. The public goods you intend to restore. The wars you will refuse.
**Tell us what government is for.**
**Tell us what America owes its people, and what America owes the world.**
Don't just tell us what we are fighting against.
Tell us what all this fighting is for.
Because if you're asking the public to fight like democracy itself is on the line, then offer us a democracy worth fighting for.

Millions of Americans have spent these years marching, organizing, donating, knocking doors, sitting through meetings, defending their neighbors from raids, reporting abuses, unionizing workplaces, protecting migrants and building mutual-aid networks from scratch. The fierce public already exists. DC, and folks aspiring to be there, should not mistake our dedication and endurance for an inexhaustible resource. Movements eventually ask a question: Toward what? You cannot organize a population forever around preventing catastrophe. "Stop the worst thing from happening" is an emergency instruction. It is not a vision of a civilization. People will defend institutions far more fiercely when those institutions visibly defend them. People will endure sacrifice when they can see what the sacrifice is for. And people who have spent years fighting merely to hold the line are entitled to ask where, eventually, we intend to go. So, Ro: Your five are good. Now give us fifty. Not fifty bills -- give us the principles. Give us the structural reforms you will fight for. The abuses you intend to investigate. The institutions you intend to rebuild. The concentrations of power you believe no democracy should tolerate. The rights you consider non-negotiable. The public goods you intend to restore. The wars you will refuse. Tell us what government is for. Tell us what America owes its people, and what America owes the world. Don't just tell us what we are fighting against. Tell us what all this fighting is for. Because if you're asking the public to fight like democracy itself is on the line, then offer us a democracy worth fighting for. name: Jeff Bridges
subject: From a hole in the ground to 54 homes
body:
Today I put my hand on a building that would not exist without a bill I passed. I don’t quite know how to describe how rewarding it felt.

| | | | | | | [View this email in your browser](https://mailchi.mp/680b77f7a949/get-more-smarter-on-colorados-budget-10379095?e=b48bb2b4f4)
---
[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/vii9oePnXK3?e=b48bb2b4f4&c2id=bbe572662fdb5fed2d0855c1bcb00da8)
| | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | Hi there,
Last year, I broke ground in Frisco on a new workforce housing project called The Scout. Today, I came back and cut the ribbon. Not much more than a hole in the ground last year is now 54 homes for people living and working in Summit County.
---
|
---
| | It took Frisco, Summit County, the Department of Local Affairs, the NHP Foundation, and Colorado’s Middle-Income Housing Authority to get it built. That last one, MIHA, is the authority I created back in 2022 through the hardest legislative fight of my ten years in office.

Weeks of drafting. Emails back and forth at all hours of the night negotiating more than 60 amendments. Getting stuck. Finding a path forward. Getting stuck again.
**Today I put my hand on a building that would not exist without that work. I don’t quite know how to describe how rewarding it felt. Teachers. First responders. Nurses. Town employees. People who keep their community running now have a home they can afford.**
---
|
---
| | Housing costs, especially in our mountain communities, have gotten so high that people who work there often can’t afford to live there. Most make too much to qualify for traditional low-income housing, but nowhere near enough to afford market rents.
**That’s exactly the gap Scout was built to fill.**
Those late night drafting sessions didn’t build The Scout on their own. A whole lot of other people made that happen. And there's a lot more housing we need to build in Colorado, especially in places where the people we depend on can't afford to live.
And that's what I plan to work on as Treasurer—building more homes like the Scout.
---
| | Talk soon,
ps This weekend we're hitting the road with Phil and Joe! Stay tuned!

name: Ruben Gallego
subject: No regrets, Peter
disclaimer_text: Paid For By Gallego for Arizona
body:
I think this is the right thing to do
#

Peter —
When I launched my campaign for Senate on January 23rd, 2023, I didn’t know what it would look like.
I knew it was going to mean a ton of time away from my family. I knew it’d take a lot of work. And I knew I’d need to raise a lot of money if I was going to have any chance at winning.
But from the beginning, I wanted to run my campaign on small donations from ordinary people because that’s exactly who I was running to represent.
I had to take a leap of faith.
The response from Arizonans was incredible. In the first week, I received donations from people up and down the state. Kathryn, a pilot from Tuscon, chipped in $15. Mike, who works in IT in Phoenix, chipped in $3. Karen, a music teacher from Peoria, gave $22.
I never had any regrets, and I never looked back.
I have an inbox too, and I know it's not always fun to receive these emails. I get it. But I’m passionate about the way we fund our campaign, because it means the people I’m accountable to are you.
Now, with a legally required FEC deadline coming up in just 5 days, I have to ask again. [**Will you chip in $5 today to help us keep the lights on and keep up our work in the Senate?**](https://act.gallegoforarizona.com/go/1000?c0=ruben-em-sep26.HW03bQ&refcode=em260925-1-subs&t=4&akid=4211%2E734936%2Ennn-y4)

name: Governor Abigail Spanberger
subject: I married Adam 20 years ago.
disclaimer_text: Paid for by United for Virginia's Future PAC
body:
Every Virginian deserves the freedom to marry the person they love.

---
| | | | Peter,
---
I married Adam more than 20 years ago in Charlottesville. Every day since has been the adventure of a lifetime– we’ve made countless moves, changed jobs, and are parents to three amazing girls. Our marriage has been the foundation of it all.
But just six months after Adam and I got married, Virginia voters passed the Marshall-Newman Amendment, a constitutional ban on marriage for same-sex couples. While a Supreme Court decision has affirmed the right to same-sex marriage at the national level, the 2006 ban is still in Virginia’s constitution.
This November, we can come together as a Commonwealth and fix that. The marriage equality amendment would repeal Virginia's ban on marriage for same-sex couples, and replace it with an affirmative guarantee that the government must treat all marriages equally under the law.
I want Virginia’s marriage equality amendment to pass with overwhelming support, and that’s why I'm rolling up my sleeves and campaigning hard for it as Governor.
[**_I hope you’ll join me in fueling this work. It takes organizing, telling our stories and talking to voters. Every day since has been the adventure of a lifetime– we’ve made countless moves, changed jobs, and are parents to three amazing girls. Our marriage has been the foundation of it all. But just six months after Adam and I got married, Virginia voters passed the Marshall-Newman Amendment, a constitutional ban on marriage for same-sex couples. While a Supreme Court decision has affirmed the right to same-sex marriage at the national level, the 2006 ban is still in Virginia’s constitution. This November, we can come together as a Commonwealth and fix that. **Washington's Debt Keeps Growing. What Could That Mean for Your Retirement?**

The math isn't complicated. A $38 trillion national debt doesn't get paid off with a speech — it gets inflated away, and the people holding cash and paper assets absorb the cost.

For retirement savers 55 and up, that's not an abstract economic debate. It's the difference between a nest egg that keeps pace and one that quietly loses ground every year, even while the account balance looks "fine" on a statement.

Physical gold has held real value through currency devaluations, recessions, and political dysfunction for longer than any fiat currency has existed. Capital Rotation — September 25, 2026
The Yield Story Didn't Need a Headline This Time. That's the Point.
Oil rose despite a concrete Iran peace proposal. Yields hit fresh multi-decade highs for the third straight session, on no single catalyst — the most consistent trend this month, and the one investors may be underweighting.
|
---
| | What Moved
---|---
**Verified fact:** Thursday's equity session was essentially flat — S&P; 500 -0.07%, Nasdaq -0.06%, Dow -0.32% — while WTI crude rose 1.04% to $93.12 and Brent rose 1.53% to $104.70. The 10-year Treasury yield hit 5.192%, its highest since 2007, and the 30-year yield reached 5.476%, its highest since 2004.
| | Rotation Signal 01 — Oil Rose Despite, Not Because of, Thursday's Diplomatic News
---|---
**Our interpretation:** Iran's concrete seven-day Hormuz proposal would, on its face, argue for lower oil prices on rising odds of resolution. That oil rose instead suggests markets are weighting Rubio's skepticism (“not a major breakthrough”) and the unresolved sequencing dispute more heavily than the proposal's existence — a more cautious read than the market's reaction to news over the past two weeks.
| | Rotation Signal 02 — The Yield Story Is Now the Single Most Consistent Trend This Month
---|---
**Verified fact:** Thursday marked the third consecutive session of fresh multi-decade highs across the yield curve, with the 30-year now at its highest level since 2004. **Our interpretation:** across three sessions this week, equities have moved on diplomatic and corporate-specific news (Meta's AI announcement, oil headlines), while Treasury yields have climbed steadily regardless of the day's other news — the most durable, singular trend this newsletter has identified all month, and arguably more consequential for broad portfolio positioning than any single day's Iran or China headline.
| | Rotation Signal 03 — A Trade Truce Extension Removes Near-Term Tail Risk Without Resolving the Setup
---|---
**Current classification: PRESSURE deferred, not resolved, on both the China and Iran tracks; CONFIRMATION of a structural yield repricing.** Semiconductor and rare-earth-exposed names likely got a genuine, if temporary, reprieve from the January 10 extension; energy-sensitive positioning got a more ambiguous signal, given oil rose despite ostensibly positive Iran news.
| | What to Watch This Week
---|---
Whether the 10- and 30-year yields continue climbing into next week absent any new catalyst, which would further confirm this as a structural, not headline-driven, move; and how markets ultimately price Iran's Hormuz proposal once Washington's formal response, if any, becomes public.

name: Jamie Raskin
subject: Before the next phase of this race, I need to ask you something
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Chris Pappas for Senate
body:
I’ve had the privilege of serving alongside Chris Pappas, and I want to tell you directly why I believe he is exactly the kind of leader we need more of in Washington.
[](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260925_3.uKFPmM&refcode=em20260925-3&t=1&akid=9151%2E582294%2ED7Pvzo)
Hi, it’s Jamie Raskin.
I’m writing to you today about my colleague and friend Chris Pappas because I’ve had the privilege of serving alongside him in Congress, and I want you to hear directly from me why this race matters.
**In the day-to-day work of Congress, you learn quickly who is there to perform and who is there to serve. Chris is firmly in the latter category.**
He shows up, does the work, and never loses sight of who sent him there.
I’ve seen him approach complex and often contentious issues with a kind of calm integrity that is increasingly rare in our politics – including as a co-sponsor of the DISCLOSE Act – which Chris championed to bring greater transparency to our elections so voters can see who is trying to buy their democracy.
It may not be a flashy issue, but it’s foundational. And that’s exactly the kind of issue Chris champions.
We are living through a genuine test of democratic self-government. That makes it all the more important to have members of Congress who understand that their job is to repair, not to inflame; to build, not to divide; to govern, not to perform.
**Chris Pappas does that work. I’ve trusted him as a colleague, and I believe he’ll bring that same steady, principled leadership to the Senate.**
**[Will you join me in supporting Chris Pappas for Senate by chipping in $5 or more right now?](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260925_3.uKFPmM&refcode=em20260925-3&t=2&akid=9151%2E582294%2ED7Pvzo)**
**[Donate $5 »](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260925_3.uKFPmM&amount=5&refcode=em20260925-3&t=21&akid=9151%2E582294%2ED7Pvzo)**
Good people don’t win these races on their own. They win because people like you decide that the kind of leadership we need is worth fighting for.
**[Please make a contribution to support Chris Pappas’s campaign for the United States Senate today.](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260925_3.uKFPmM&refcode=em20260925-3&t=22&akid=9151%2E582294%2ED7Pvzo)**
Very truly yours,
Jamie Raskin

Friends,
The last few months have been extraordinary. I've criss-crossed the state and listened to thousands of Kansans talk about their challenges, their struggles, their hopes and their dreams. And now, we're in the home stretch. **Early voting in Kansas starts October 14, and Election Day is on November 3rd. That means there are less than 40 days remaining to decide the future of our state and our country.**
We're in the final stretch of this race, and I'm not going to stop. I'll spend every day from now until November 3rd traveling and talking to Kansans throughout our state -- Republicans, Democrats, and independents alike. I'm going to do that because that's how I started, and it's how I mean to go on: as a leader who shows up for every single person, regardless of their political party, and fights every single day to make their lives better.
Still, as the election draws ever closer, I can't help but think about how differently my opponent, Sen. Roger Marshall, and I approach leadership.
* Marshall decided listening to Kansans was "dangerous" and "non-productive" -- and stopped holding public town halls.
* He voted to cut food and healthcare assistance to thousands of vulnerable Kansans.
* He used taxpayer money to fund multiple trips to Florida, where he owns a waterfront home.
* He backed the tariffs that are costing Kansas families as much as $200 or more a month for everyday necessities.
* He supported the war in Iran, and now gas is over a dollar/gallon more than it was a year ago -- and diesel is at a record high and climbing.

I could go on, but you get the point: **Kansas -- and the country -- deserves better. We can do better. And we must.**
Folks, leaders must put the people they represent ahead of their own interests. To do that, though, a leader has to be willing to show up and _listen_ to people. Hear their struggles. Think critically about solutions. And courageously stand up for them, even when it's hard.
I've spent my life doing that. And if I'm elected, I'll _keep_ doing it. I'll work with Democrats, Republicans and Independents alike to make housing affordable, get healthcare costs under control, protect the security Kansas seniors have earned, lower costs for Kansas families and stand up against the corruption and chaos in Washington.
After listening to thousands of voters, I know Kansans are fired up and ready for change. Everywhere I go, Republicans tell me they've never voted for a Democrat -- but they're going to vote for me. A recent poll shows me leading Roger Marshall by 2 points. Election experts at RealClearPolling just shifted this race to "Toss Up" status. The New York Times even listed it as one of the most competitive in the country.
**[I know we can win this, beat Marshall and bring our fight for Kansans to the Senate. But with less than 40 days to go, it's more important to me than ever to keep listening. So please, will you take 60 seconds to share your thoughts with me?](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/32ab8baa-0e89-4a41-b98e-3fe942d80b6e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
[Survey](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/32ab8baa-0e89-4a41-b98e-3fe942d80b6e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Thank you,
Adam Hamilton
_P.S. -- The strength of our grassroots movement is amazing to witness -- and it's no accident. We're powered by more than 50,000 grassroots supporters who believe in what we're building. But Roger Marshall is backed by huge corporate PACs, and he and his allies have spent nearly $7.5 million so far to protect the status quo. **[Can you chip in anything you can spare to help us meet this moment and stay in the fight?](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/84343378-7507-4144-ba41-26855af116cb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** Thank you for standing with me!_

body:
Local election offices need people ready to serve their communities. | |
---
Peter, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement are attempting to undermine our elections and our democracy through their election denial. This includes degrading election infrastructure and trust in the system, while going as far as threatening election officials. This has made it more difficult for counties to recruit poll workers, both in the last presidential election and in the fast-approaching midterms. **When the polls open on November 3, it is critical that members of the community are there to welcome the first voters.** Official county poll workers will check people in, hand out ballots, answer questions, and help their neighbors cast their votes. Election Day depends on that work. Poll workers are critical public servants. But local election offices are having a hard time recruiting enough people to do it. Poll workers help keep in-person voting accessible for people with disabilities, voters who need language assistance, people without reliable access to mail, and anyone who wants to vote at their polling place. Every voter who comes through the door deserves help without judgment. **At OnePA, we’re working with creators and community voices to share key election dates and poll worker resources. We’re asking you to be part of that work by serving your neighbors on Election Day.** [**Sign up to be a poll worker and help your local election office prepare for November 3, so that when your neighbors arrive to vote, someone is there to welcome them, answer their questions, and help keep the polling place running.**](https://click.actionnetwork.org/ss/c/u001.XaF8mXqsA6b2dSPmhsleMSiWfddei9CkIuGojyn4RzV-JR_4G50wTT0Ck55_WUiUMatjsdaUDjbzOQegIzfaKXNNiwYULZpIp6dMdbAcOrOUoq7lcXZgP2rR60QJpmjoelGp7tJrkAcO-Ex0Y3L_ljiQh1urkB9wmcX7Z5NywUdlSDUz_FsBtv3u4o8dBrH_ANX9oSYdGLArexSivr7FhV9uz7E8tS1L-Be2wxefuj-pSJvT8gsg6Oj40g4souRAQy83ph-T9Lf2TEeXWk4hNGhB8jN6rJ7rn7qThHMNfek/4uc/o2LZl4cjTkOstuBSWd3RKw/h0/h001.4qf73gH9geehSUylsfwk7Fd6yQm9Y5l-wzdv7B0-2tY) | | [SIGN UP TO BE A POLL WORKER](https://click.actionnetwork.org/ss/c/u001.XaF8mXqsA6b2dSPmhsleMSiWfddei9CkIuGojyn4RzVQc5PUf5PxYiWRs4Wt6TtYdvQgKro4YLlyk0wJC1iVpJaQN5bCfP4Iq7T6aZZ0fBu4-cxpZDTM_HWd1mDnoerriQ1p4-sO8uoVYrpL4wmygZPH3Rbe_w2RlDISPNvX-l2Fsd7wZ7yQGI_aX8fC4sEFeCtk7IsCbW4P-7nyLwomRroe8AsYEYqWF9PakNYn5dUovxCYy4Oyzra4TnQgQBCGfFCcpolMMNBdVj_MIY4-INlyz7lmBzONFIAhpTagdfg/4uc/o2LZl4cjTkOstuBSWd3RKw/h1/h001.x5PHw9H7KEI7RVLeGOH43_Lm1niM4qpKFMV43U-jqKg)
